newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK's Tung, Rifkind no closer to meeting of minds.
newsitem.headline: HK's Tung, Rifkind no closer to meeting of minds.

text.p: Hong Kong's future leader Tung Chee-hwa met British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind for the first time since Tung's appointment but reported no narrowing in the gulf between the outgoing and incoming administrations.
Tung told reporters after the talks on Sunday that Britain had not budged in its refusal to aid the provisional legislature that China intends to install upon the handover.
Hong Kong, a British colony for more than 150 years, reverts to China at midnight on June 30, 1997.
"On the work of the provisional legislature, I've urged the Hong Kong government to give assistance and help," Tung said.
"Britain's position has always been clear, but I hope they will reconsider," he told reporters.

Britain argues that the formation of the provisional legislature, set up by a China-appointed panel in December to replace the elected chamber, is illegal under the terms of the 1984 Sino-British handover treaty on Hong Kong.
It has challenged China to let the World Court rule on the legality of the body. China has flatly rejected the proposal.

Britain has refused to assist the body, which is expected to roll back democratic reforms sponsored by British Governor Chris Patten to China's fury. The legislature was returned in 1995 under the reforms that China plans to reverse.

Rifkind, whose visit was curtailed so that he can return early to London for a key parliamentary vote, spent just under an hour with Tung and has meetings scheduled with the colonial administration and Hong Kong politicians.
He landed in the eye of a bitter political storm over the future of democratic elections and human rights laws, which China plans to dilute after July 1.
Rifkind criticised China's plans for the laws, which he said undermined confidence in Hong Kong.

"These are aspects of Chinese policy which inevitably have damaged confidence in the territory and the only way that that confidence can be fully restored is by a fundamental change in that policy," Rifkind said when he landed in Hong Kong on Saturday.
Tung said he planned to listen to views in Hong Kong about how to proceed in amending the laws, but said he would hold to his own values and beliefs.
"There'll be consultation. I think I would listen very carefully to the voice of these consultations," he said.
"But on the other hand , I have a set of values and beliefs which I will hold on to them very much," he said.

Tung, chosen by a China-backed Selection Committee in December, argues the planned changes are merely technicalities and points to Hong Kong's buoyant economy as proof that confidence in the territory's post-1997 future is high.
